newsitem.title: USA: Calif. shareholder suit measure weakens in polls.
newsitem.headline: Calif. shareholder suit measure weakens in polls.

text.p: California's Proposition 211, which would reduce obstacles to filing shareholder lawsuits, is headed for defeat in tomorrow's election, according to opponents of the measure.

They said most recent opinion polls indicate the controversial proposal, which would also expand the definition of fraud and lift restrictions on fees of lawyers bringing shareholder lawsuits, will fail.

George Sollman, president and chairman of Centigram Communications Corp and chairman of the American Electronics Association (AEA) trade group, said the latest poll showed 54 percent of likely voters opposing 211.
That poll, as of October 30, showed 28 percent in favor of the measure and 18 percent undecided.

The measure is one of California's most contentious ballot issues. An estimated $55 million has been raised in the battle over 211 -- $35 million by opponents, including a blue-ribbon list of Silicon Valley high-tech and biotech companies, and $20 million by lawyers and other supporters.

President Clionton, Republican presidential candidate Bob Dole and Securities and Exchange Commission Chairman Arthur Levitt have come out against the measure. Levitt said 211 would make California "a magnet for class action suits."
Nearly half the AEA's high tech member firms have said in a survey they would consider leaving California if the initiative passes.
Some economists have warned the measure could have a damaging effect on the national economy.

A study last month by the Economic Strategy Institute in Washington projected that passage of 211 could result in a loss of up to 1.8 million jobs and a net loss to U.S. gross domestic product of up to $102 billion.

The study, by well-known trade economist Clyde Prestowitz, president of the institute, projects that a damaging increase in what the industry considers to be "frivolous lawsuits" would result in a 12 to 24 percent drop in stock market values.
Opponents of 211 also argue that laws on the books already protect investors against fraud.
They say 211 would allow lawyers to file suits in California that have been barred from federal courts by 1995 federal securities law reform legislation.
"It's a full-time employment act for class action securities litigators," said Sollman.
Proponents of 211, including lawyers who bring shareholder lawsuits, say they drew up the measure when it was clear that anti-business sentiment appeared to be strong in California.
They say 211 would help people recover from major securities fraud.

Opponents of 211, who have appealed to Wall Street for financial support, say the measure could have a dampening effect on the ability of corporate officers, who would become personally liable under the measure, to provide forward-looking remarks.
This, in turn, would increase uncertainty and investor risk related to the already highly-volatile technology sector, they say.
